subject: Banking
title: Who Pays for Bank Failures?
description: A 60-second lesson on Who Pays for Bank Failures?.

hook.text: Bank failures cost someone money. The question is always who: shareholders, depositors, other banks, or taxpayers.

buildup.text: Shareholders are hit first, but insured deposits, rescue funds, and bank fees spread losses much wider.

discovery.text: In practice the bill travels through the FDIC, emergency backstops, and then into taxes, fees, or lower returns.

twist.text: Banks pass their FDIC premiums to customers through lower rates and higher fees. Customers always pay in the end.

climax.text: The cost of bank failures is always shared across the economy. The only question is how visibly and how fairly.

punchline.text: Shareholders lose first. Taxpayers bail out last. Customers pay through fees.

quiz.question: How are FDIC premiums ultimately funded?
options: Banks pay premiums but pass costs to customers through fees

details.summary: Bank failures are paid for through a combination of shareholder wipeout, bondholder losses, deposit insurance fund assessments on surviving banks, and sometimes direct taxpayer bailouts when the failure is large enough to threaten the system.
details.whyItMatters: Understanding who ultimately pays for bank failures exposes the hidden subsidies in banking. When deposit insurance funds run low, surviving banks pay special assessments that are ultimately passed to customers through higher fees.
takeaways: Shareholders lose everything first in a bank failure
The FDIC fund is replenished by assessments on all surviving insured banks
Taxpayers become the ultimate backstop when failures exceed the insurance fund

faq.question: Does the FDIC fund have enough money to cover bank failures?
faq.answer: The fund held $128 billion in early 2023 against $18 trillion in insured deposits. It can handle individual failures but would be overwhelmed by multiple large bank failures simultaneously. In that scenario, the Treasury provides a backstop.

faq.question: Are bank customers indirectly paying for failures?
faq.answer: Yes. When the FDIC charges special assessments to replenish its fund, banks pass these costs to customers through higher fees and lower deposit rates. The 2023 bank failures resulted in a $16 billion special assessment on surviving banks.
